question: On Mount Carmel, Elijah challenged 450 prophets of Baal to a contest: each side prepares a bull on an altar; the god who answers with fire wins the contest. The Baal prophets danced and slashed themselves all morning. Nothing. Elijah drenched his altar with twelve jars of water until the trench overflowed, prayed once, and fire fell from heaven consuming bull, wood, stones, and water. What did Elijah do with the prophets of Baal afterward?
answer: All 450 were seized and killed at the Brook Kishon
choices: All 450 were seized and killed at the Brook Kishon
They were exiled to the desert of Edom forever
They were forced to rebuild the altar of the Lord
They were chained to Baal's temple in Samaria
context: 1 Kings 18. King Ahab and Queen Jezebel had introduced Baal worship into Israel; Jezebel was killing the prophets of the Lord. Elijah taunted the prophets that perhaps Baal was traveling or asleep. After the fire fell, Elijah ran ahead of Ahab's chariot in the rain — only to flee for his life when Jezebel vowed to kill him. The next chapter has Elijah hearing God in the 'still small voice' on Mount Horeb.

question: Queen Esther, a secretly Jewish girl who had won the king's favor, learned that the king's grand vizier Haman had decreed every Jew in Persia be killed on a single day. Esther fasted three days, then approached the king's throne uninvited (a capital offense) and invited the king and Haman to a private banquet. At the second banquet she finally accused Haman, naming him in front of the king. Haman was hanged that night on the very gallows he had built for Esther's cousin Mordecai. What was the height of those gallows?
answer: Fifty cubits — about 75 feet high
choices: Fifty cubits — about 75 feet high
Twelve cubits — the height of the palace gate
One hundred cubits — taller than the temple roof
Three cubits — a common scaffold height
context: The Book of Esther is the only book of the Bible that does not directly name God. Mordecai had earlier told Esther: 'Who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?' (Esther 4:14). The festival of Purim, still celebrated, commemorates the rescue.

question: King Belshazzar of Babylon held a great feast for a thousand of his nobles and ordered the gold and silver vessels his father Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the Jerusalem Temple brought in, so the guests could drink wine from them while praising Babylonian gods. At that moment a disembodied hand appeared and wrote four words in fiery letters on the palace wall. Belshazzar's face turned pale and his knees knocked together. None of his wise men could read the writing — only Daniel, brought from prison, could. What four words did the hand write?
answer: MENE MENE TEKEL UPHARSIN
choices: MENE MENE TEKEL UPHARSIN
ASHUR BAAL MARDUK ANU
AZAZEL LILITH MOLOCH DAGON
BABEL NIMROD CHEDOR SHINAR
context: Daniel translated: 'Numbered, numbered, weighed, divided' — God had numbered Belshazzar's reign and found it wanting; the kingdom was being divided between the Medes and Persians. That same night Babylon fell to Cyrus the Great's army (539 BC); Belshazzar was killed. The story is in Daniel 5; 'the writing on the wall' became the proverb for unmistakable warning.

question: Job was the wealthiest man in the East — seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, ten children, and a name for righteousness. Satan argued before God that Job only loved God because God blessed him. God let Satan take everything. In one day messengers came: raiders stole his oxen, fire burned his sheep, raiders took his camels, and a great wind collapsed his eldest son's house on all ten children. Then Job was struck with painful boils. What did Job say?
answer: The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away, blessed be His name
choices: The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away, blessed be His name
Why has the Lord forsaken his servant in this hour of pain
Show me my sin, that I may know what I have done wrong
Remember my children, though the wealth itself is nothing
context: Job 1:21. The exact phrasing: 'Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return — the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.' His wife told him to 'curse God and die.' His three friends Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar sat with him in silence seven days before insisting his suffering must be punishment for hidden sin — which Job rejected. God finally answered Job from a whirlwind, asking questions about creation (Job 38-41) that ended Job's questions. God then restored Job double — fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, seven sons and three daughters.

question: King Ahab of Israel coveted a vineyard next to his palace in Jezreel. The owner, Naboth, refused to sell: it was his ancestral land, forbidden by law to transfer. Ahab went home and sulked on his bed, refusing to eat. His Phoenician queen Jezebel mocked him and said she would handle it. She wrote letters in Ahab's name ordering the elders of Jezreel to proclaim a fast, seat Naboth at the head of the people, and bring two false witnesses against him. What did Jezebel have the witnesses claim Naboth had said?
answer: That Naboth had cursed God and the king
choices: That Naboth had cursed God and the king
That Naboth had worshipped Baal in secret
That Naboth had stolen from the royal treasury
That Naboth had plotted with Aram against Ahab
context: Naboth was taken outside the city and stoned to death (1 Kings 21). Ahab took possession. The prophet Elijah confronted him in the vineyard with: 'Have you killed and also taken possession?' — and prophesied that dogs would lick Ahab's blood in that same spot and devour Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel. Both prophecies came to pass.

question: Walking on his palace roof in Jerusalem, King David saw Bathsheba bathing — wife of Uriah the Hittite, one of his mighty men away at war. David slept with her; she conceived. David recalled Uriah, hoping he would sleep with his wife. Uriah refused. David sent him back with a sealed letter to General Joab ordering Uriah placed at the fiercest point of the siege and abandoned. Uriah died. The prophet Nathan came to David with a parable about a rich man stealing a poor man's only beloved ewe lamb. What did Nathan say when David condemned the rich man?
answer: You are the man, said Nathan to David
choices: You are the man, said Nathan to David
You have done what no king should do
Your sin will return upon your house
Repent, and the Lord may yet forgive
context: 2 Samuel 11-12. David repented (writing Psalm 51, 'Have mercy upon me, O God'). But the child of the adultery died. Nathan also prophesied that the sword would never depart from David's house — fulfilled in the rape of David's daughter Tamar by his son Amnon, Amnon's murder by his brother Absalom, and Absalom's later revolt and death.

question: Hannah, one of two wives of Elkanah, had no children. Her rival wife Peninnah taunted her about it year after year. At the annual pilgrimage to the tabernacle at Shiloh, Hannah went alone to the doorpost and prayed silently, her lips moving without sound, weeping bitterly. The priest Eli, watching, assumed she was drunk and rebuked her. She explained she was pouring out her soul to God. She vowed that if she bore a son, she would dedicate him to God's service for life. She bore the son. What did she name him?
answer: Samuel
choices: Samuel
Solomon
Joshua
Joseph
context: The story is in 1 Samuel 1-2. The name Samuel means 'asked of God.' Hannah's prayer of thanksgiving (1 Samuel 2:1-10, 'My heart exults in the Lord') is a clear model for Mary's Magnificat in Luke 1. Samuel grew up at Shiloh, heard God call his name in the night while he slept beside the Ark, and became the prophet who anointed both Saul and David as kings. Once Samuel was weaned, Hannah brought him to Eli and left him to serve at the sanctuary.

question: When the Assyrian king Sennacherib marched on Jerusalem in 701 BC with the largest army the ancient Near East had seen, King Hezekiah took an extraordinary precaution. He had workmen carve a tunnel through 1,750 feet of solid rock under the City of David, bringing fresh water from the Gihon Spring outside the walls to the Pool of Siloam inside. Two teams started from opposite ends and met in the middle. What did Hezekiah do with the spring's outside opening once the tunnel was finished?
answer: Sealed and hid it so the Assyrians could find no water
choices: Sealed and hid it so the Assyrians could find no water
Poisoned it with hyssop and salt to sicken the besiegers
Diverted it to flood the Assyrian camp in the valley
Left it open to draw the Assyrians into ambush
context: 2 Chronicles 32:30 records the waterworks; the tunnel still exists today and tourists wade through it. The commemorative inscription found in 1880 describes the two teams hearing each other's pickaxes through the rock. The Assyrian army was destroyed outside the walls — 'the angel of the Lord went out and struck down 185,000' (2 Kings 19:35). Sennacherib went home and was murdered by two of his own sons in the temple of Nisroch.

question: Nehemiah, cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes, was granted leave in 445 BC to rebuild Jerusalem's broken walls (a ruin for 142 years since Nebuchadnezzar's destruction). He rode out by night to assess the damage, then organized the people in family groups to rebuild section by section. The Samaritan governor Sanballat and the Ammonite official Tobiah mocked openly and then plotted armed attack. How did Nehemiah's workers continue building under threat?
answer: Each man worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other
choices: Each man worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other
They worked only at night and slept inside the city by day
They hired Persian mercenaries to guard each section of wall
They paid Sanballat tribute money to let them finish in peace
context: Nehemiah 4:17. The wall was completed in only 52 days, despite plots, threats, and starvation wages that nearly caused internal revolt. Nehemiah also dramatically denounced the wealthy for charging interest on loans to their own destitute brothers, forcing them to swear restoration. The completed walls were dedicated with two great choirs walking the ramparts in opposite directions.

question: Under King Darius the Mede, the elderly Hebrew official Daniel was promoted over all other satraps. Jealous officials tricked the king into signing a thirty-day decree that anyone praying to any god but Darius would be thrown to the lions — and the king could not revoke it. Daniel kept praying at his open window toward Jerusalem three times a day. He was thrown into the pit and the stone sealed with the king's signet. Darius spent the night fasting and ran to the den at dawn. What did Daniel call up to him?
answer: My God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths
choices: My God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths
Bless the king who delivered me from death
I wrestled the lions and made them my servants
The spirits of my fathers stood between us
context: Daniel 6:21-22. Darius then commanded that the conspirators who had accused Daniel — together with their wives and children — be thrown into the same den; the lions devoured them before they hit the floor. Darius issued a new decree that all in his kingdom should tremble before the God of Daniel. Daniel lived on into the reign of Cyrus.

question: When God ordered the reluctant prophet Jonah to go preach repentance to Israel's bitter enemy Nineveh, Jonah instead booked passage on a ship heading the opposite direction, toward Tarshish in Spain. God sent a violent storm; the terrified pagan sailors cast lots to find who was responsible, and the lot fell on Jonah, asleep below decks. He confessed and told them to throw him overboard. They reluctantly did so — the sea immediately calmed. A great fish swallowed Jonah whole. How long was Jonah inside the fish?
answer: Three days and three nights
choices: Three days and three nights
One day and one night
Seven days and seven nights
Forty days and forty nights
context: Jonah 1-2. Jonah prayed from inside the fish; the fish vomited him onto dry land. He preached to Nineveh ('Forty days more and Nineveh shall be overthrown!'); the Ninevites repented from the king down to the cattle wearing sackcloth, and God spared the city. Jonah sulked under a withered gourd plant. The 'three days and three nights' phrase was applied by Jesus to his own coming three days in the tomb (Matthew 12:40).

question: After waiting until he was 100 years old for the son God had promised, Abraham was tested when God told him to take that son — Isaac — to Mount Moriah and offer him as a burnt sacrifice. Abraham rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey, took two servants and Isaac, and traveled three days. Isaac carried the wood for his own pyre up the mountain. As Abraham raised the knife over his bound son on the altar, an angel called from heaven to stop him. Abraham looked up. What did he see caught by its horns in a thicket?
answer: A ram, which he sacrificed in place of Isaac
choices: A ram, which he sacrificed in place of Isaac
A turtledove, which he released as an offering
A young bull, which he led down to a level place
A lamb still bearing its mother's milk
context: Genesis 22. Abraham named the place 'The Lord will provide.' Isaac, on the way up, had asked his father where the lamb for the offering was; Abraham answered: 'God himself will provide the lamb.' The episode is read by Jews on Rosh Hashanah and is called the Akedah ('binding'). Christians from the earliest centuries read Isaac carrying the wood up the mountain as a foreshadowing of Christ carrying the cross.

question: Returning home after twenty years of working for his uncle Laban, Jacob feared his estranged brother Esau — whom he had cheated of birthright and blessing. Hearing Esau was coming with 400 men, Jacob sent his family and flocks across the river Jabbok and stayed alone on the far bank that night. A mysterious man wrestled with him until dawn. Unable to overpower Jacob, the man touched the socket of Jacob's hip, dislocating it. Jacob refused to release him without a blessing. The stranger asked Jacob's name, then renamed him — saying he had striven with God and humans and prevailed. What new name did the stranger give Jacob?
answer: Israel
choices: Israel
Reuben
Benjamin
Joseph
context: Genesis 32:22-32. The name 'Israel' means 'he who strives with God' or 'God strives.' Jacob limped from then on; Jewish tradition still does not eat the sciatic nerve from the hip-socket of animals in remembrance. Jacob renamed the place Peniel ('face of God'): 'I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.' The next morning Esau, far from attacking, ran to meet Jacob and embraced him.

question: Samson, an Israelite judge of supernatural strength, had killed a thousand Philistines with the jawbone of a donkey and torn down city gates with his bare hands. His enemies could not defeat him by force, so they paid the Philistine woman Delilah eleven hundred pieces of silver to discover the secret of his strength. Three times she asked; three times Samson lied (fresh bowstrings, new ropes, weaving his hair). The fourth time, worn down by her constant nagging, he told the truth — and while he slept on her lap, she had a servant cut what?
answer: His seven long braids of hair
choices: His seven long braids of hair
The leather of his sandals
The cord of his Nazirite cloak
The sinews of his bowstring
context: Judges 16. Samson was a Nazirite from birth — vowed never to cut his hair, drink wine, or touch a corpse. His hair was the visible sign of that vow. The Philistines blinded him, set him to grinding grain in prison. At a Philistine feast in the temple of Dagon, with his hair grown back, Samson asked to lean between the two main pillars — and pulled the temple down on himself and three thousand Philistines, killing more in his death than in his life.

question: Called to free Israel from Midianite raiders, Gideon assembled 32,000 men. God told him the army was too large; victory would seem human. Gideon sent home anyone afraid; 22,000 left. Still too many. God ordered Gideon to take the remaining 10,000 to a stream and watch how they drank. Those who knelt and lapped were sent home; those who scooped water in cupped hands to drink while keeping their eyes up were kept. With those 300 Gideon attacked at midnight. What did each man carry besides his sword?
answer: A trumpet and a clay jar with a lit torch hidden inside
choices: A trumpet and a clay jar with a lit torch hidden inside
A bow and a quiver of seven flaming arrows
A long spear and a small bronze shield
A wooden club and a leather sling with stones
context: Judges 7. Surrounding the Midianite camp, Gideon's 300 simultaneously broke their jars (revealing the torches), blew the trumpets, and shouted 'A sword for the Lord and for Gideon!' The terrified Midianites turned on each other in the dark and fled. Gideon refused to be made king afterward: 'The Lord will rule over you.'

question: Crossing the Jordan River into the Promised Land, Joshua's army faced the walled city of Jericho first. God gave Joshua unusual orders. For six days the Israelite army was to march around the city in silence, with seven priests carrying ram's-horn trumpets walking before the Ark of the Covenant. On the seventh day they were to march around the city seven times. Then the priests would blow a long blast, the people would give a great shout, and what would happen to the walls of Jericho?
answer: The walls would collapse outward to the ground
choices: The walls would collapse outward to the ground
The gates would unlock and swing wide open
The defenders would be struck blind on the ramparts
Fire would consume the city's wooden towers
context: Joshua 6. The walls did fall down flat; the army went straight up and took the city. Only Rahab the prostitute and her family were spared, in return for having hidden Israelite spies earlier — Rahab had marked her window with a scarlet cord. Archaeologists at the ancient mound of Jericho have debated for over a century what to make of the city's collapsed walls (radiocarbon-dated controversially).

question: Naomi, an Israelite widow whose husband and two sons died in Moab, returned to Bethlehem with her Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth, who refused to abandon her. They arrived destitute at the barley harvest. Ruth went to glean — picking up grain dropped by reapers, a legal privilege for the poor. By chance she gleaned in the field of Boaz, a wealthy kinsman of Naomi's dead husband. He noticed Ruth, asked his foreman about her, then spoke to her. What did Boaz order his reapers to do for her secretly?
answer: Pull out grain from the bundles on purpose and leave it
choices: Pull out grain from the bundles on purpose and leave it
Carry her share of grain back to Naomi at sundown
Bring her water and bread from his table at noon
Pay her wages double what they paid their own men
context: Ruth 2:16. Naomi quickly recognized that Boaz was a 'kinsman-redeemer' — under Israelite law, the closest male relative of a dead man could marry his widow and buy back his property. Ruth eventually did marry Boaz; their great-grandson would be King David. The Book of Ruth is read by Jews each year at the festival of Shavuot.

question: Two women living in the same house came before King Solomon. Each had given birth a few days apart; one baby had died in the night, smothered when his mother rolled over in her sleep. Each woman now claimed the living baby was hers. There were no witnesses. The first insisted her rival had swapped the dead infant for the live one in the dark; the second insisted just the opposite. Solomon ordered a sword brought and decreed the living baby be cut in half. What did the real mother cry out?
answer: Give her the living child, but do not kill him
choices: Give her the living child, but do not kill him
Strike him with the sword as the king has commanded
Let the wise king decide as the spirit moves him
The dead child is mine, return the other to her now
context: 1 Kings 3:16-28. Solomon gave the baby to the woman who tried to save him, declaring her the real mother — 'all Israel heard of the judgment, and they stood in awe of the king, because they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice.' Solomon had asked God for wisdom rather than wealth or long life at the start of his reign; this was the first famous proof of the answer.

question: The king of Aram, frustrated that his secret battle plans against Israel kept being thwarted, learned that the prophet Elisha was supernaturally hearing his words even in his bedroom. He sent a great army by night to capture Elisha at the city of Dothan. Elisha's young servant woke in the morning to see the city surrounded by chariots and horses and panicked. Elisha prayed: 'Lord, open his eyes that he may see.' What did the servant then see on the mountain around Elisha?
answer: The mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire
choices: The mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire
The Arameans were vanishing into a deep mist
A great host of angels with flaming swords descending
Twelve giant trees uprooting themselves to block the road
context: 2 Kings 6:8-23. Elisha then prayed that the Arameans be struck with blindness, and led the entire army into the heart of Samaria's capital — into the king of Israel's hands. The king asked if he should kill them. Elisha said no: feed them and send them home. The king set a great feast before the Arameans and sent them away; the raiding parties stopped coming. Elisha's master Elijah had earlier been taken to heaven in a similar chariot of fire (2 Kings 2).

question: Forty years after fleeing Egypt for killing an Egyptian taskmaster, Moses was eighty and tending his father-in-law Jethro's sheep on Mount Horeb. He saw a strange sight: a thorn bush burning with bright fire but not consumed. As he turned aside, a voice called his name out of the bush and told him to take off his sandals; he stood on holy ground. The voice identified itself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and ordered Moses back to Egypt to free the Israelites. When Moses asked God's name to tell the people, what did God answer?
answer: I AM WHO I AM
choices: I AM WHO I AM
I AM the Lord
I AM Elohim
I AM Most High
context: Exodus 3. The Hebrew is YHWH (the Tetragrammaton), traditionally not spoken aloud — Jews substitute 'Adonai' (Lord) when reading. Moses argued he was a poor speaker; God gave him his brother Aaron as spokesman and a wooden staff that would become a serpent and back again on demand. The staff later parted the Red Sea, brought water from rock at Meribah, and lifted high during the Israelite victory over Amalek. God told Moses to say to the people: 'I AM has sent me to you.'

question: Fifty days after the Resurrection, the eleven remaining apostles plus Matthias (chosen to replace Judas Iscariot) and about 120 disciples were gathered together in Jerusalem for the Jewish festival of Shavuot. Suddenly a sound like a violent rushing wind filled the whole house. Something appeared above each person's head and the disciples were all filled with the Holy Spirit. They poured out into the street preaching, and pilgrims from across the Mediterranean each heard them speaking in their own native languages. What appeared above each disciple's head?
answer: A tongue of flame, like many small fires
choices: A tongue of flame, like many small fires
A white dove with outstretched wings
A shining crown of seven golden stars
A flickering candle in a vessel of oil
context: The Pentecost story is in Acts 2. About three thousand people were baptized that day after Peter's sermon — the traditional birthday of the Christian Church. The languages listed include those of Parthians, Medes, Elamites, Mesopotamians, Cappadocians, Phrygians, Pamphylians, Egyptians, Libyans, Cretans, Arabs, and visitors from Rome. Some bystanders scoffed that the apostles must be drunk; Peter replied it was only the third hour of the day — about 9 a.m.

question: Saul of Tarsus, a young Pharisee who had stood watching the stoning of the first Christian martyr Stephen and held the cloaks of the killers, then began dragging Christians from their homes in Jerusalem and throwing them in prison. He obtained letters of authority from the high priest and set out for Damascus to arrest Christians there. As he neared the city around noon, a light brighter than the sun blinded him and threw him to the ground. A voice spoke to him. What did the voice say?
answer: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?
choices: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?
Stand up, Saul, your time of darkness is over
I am the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
The blood of Stephen cries against you now
context: Acts 9. Saul asked: 'Who are you, Lord?' The voice answered: 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.' Saul was led blind into Damascus, fasted three days, and was healed by a frightened disciple named Ananias whom God ordered to go to him. Saul was baptized, took the Greek form of his name (Paul), and became the apostle whose journeys carried Christianity from Judea to Rome — writing about half the New Testament along the way before being beheaded under Nero around 64-67 AD.

question: On Paul's second missionary journey, he and Silas were severely flogged and thrown into the inner prison at Philippi for casting a demon out of a slave girl whose owners profited from her fortune-telling. With their feet in stocks in the dark, they spent the night singing hymns and praying. Around midnight a violent earthquake shook the foundations. The prison doors flew open and every prisoner's chains fell off. The jailer drew his sword, ready to kill himself. What did Paul shout from inside?
answer: Do yourself no harm, we are all still here
choices: Do yourself no harm, we are all still here
Flee, jailer, while the gates are still open
Bring me bread and water before you take your life
May Christ judge those who used the lash on us
context: Acts 16:25-34. The terrified jailer fell trembling at their feet asking what he must do to be saved. He took Paul and Silas home, washed their wounds, and was baptized that night with his entire household. The next morning the magistrates ordered them released — only to learn (alarmed) that Paul and Silas were Roman citizens, illegally beaten and imprisoned. Paul demanded the magistrates come personally and escort them out, then went on to Thessalonica.

question: After feeding the five thousand on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, Jesus sent the disciples ahead in a boat while he went up a mountain alone to pray. A wind rose; by the fourth watch (around 3 a.m.) they were straining at the oars in the middle of the lake. Jesus came walking toward them on the waves. The disciples thought they saw a ghost. Peter called: 'Lord, if it is you, tell me to come.' Jesus said: 'Come.' Peter stepped out. What made him sink?
answer: He noticed the strong wind, became afraid, and began to sink
choices: He noticed the strong wind, became afraid, and began to sink
A great wave broke directly over his head as he walked
His sandal strap caught on a rope from the boat behind
He turned to call Andrew and lost his footing in fright
context: Matthew 14:22-33. Peter cried out: 'Lord, save me!' Jesus immediately reached out, caught him by the hand, and said: 'You of little faith, why did you doubt?' When they got into the boat together the wind ceased; the other disciples worshipped Jesus, saying: 'Truly you are the Son of God.' This is the only New Testament miracle of any human besides Jesus walking on water.

question: Tired from his journey through Samaria around noon, Jesus sat alone by Jacob's well outside the village of Sychar. A Samaritan woman came to draw water at the unusual midday hour, probably to avoid the other village women. Jesus asked her for a drink. She was shocked: Jews did not speak to Samaritans, and no man addressed a strange woman in public. He offered her living water. What did Jesus then reveal about her private life?
answer: She had had five husbands, and the man she lived with was not her husband
choices: She had had five husbands, and the man she lived with was not her husband
Her father had been a priest of Samaria who fell into idolatry
Her mother had been a widow forced to beg by the temple gate
Her brother had killed a man in a quarrel over goats and silver
context: John 4. The woman ran to the village calling out: 'Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did. Could this be the Messiah?' Many Samaritans believed because of her witness, then because they heard Jesus themselves. Jesus also told her that the time was coming (and was now) when true worshippers would worship God neither at Jerusalem nor at Mount Gerizim (the Samaritan holy site), but in spirit and in truth.

question: When Lazarus of Bethany fell ill, his sisters Mary and Martha sent word to Jesus, their close friend. Jesus deliberately stayed where he was two more days. By the time he arrived, Lazarus had been in the tomb four days. Martha ran out: 'Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.' Jesus said: 'I am the resurrection and the life.' Mary came next and fell at his feet. Jesus wept. He had them roll back the stone (Martha objecting at the stench) and called into the tomb. What did Jesus call out?
answer: Lazarus, come out
choices: Lazarus, come out
My friend, your sleep is over
Stand and walk in the light
By my Father, rise and live
context: John 11:43. Lazarus came out, still wrapped in linen burial cloths. Jesus said: 'Unbind him and let him go.' Many of the Jews who had come to mourn with the sisters believed in Jesus from that hour — and the report reaching the chief priests was what finally triggered the official plot to kill him. The shortest verse in the King James Bible is from this same scene: 'Jesus wept' (John 11:35).

question: As Jesus hung on the cross at Golgotha from noon to 3 p.m., darkness covered the land. Jesus cried out 'Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?' — My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Some thought he was calling for Elijah. A soldier raised a sponge of sour wine to his lips on a hyssop stalk. Jesus drank, said 'It is finished,' bowed his head, and died. At that moment the Temple curtain was torn in two from top to bottom and an earthquake shook the city. A Roman centurion stood at the foot of the cross. What did he say?
answer: Truly this man was the Son of God
choices: Truly this man was the Son of God
He was righteous, let us bury him with honor
I have never seen such suffering as this man
Surely the gods of Rome will hear of this sky
context: Mark 15:39 and Matthew 27:54. Christian tradition names the centurion Longinus and identifies him with the soldier whose spear pierced Jesus's side after the death — the Lance of Longinus. Tradition holds that Longinus later converted, returned to his native Cappadocia, and was eventually martyred for his faith. The Lance is one of the great Christian relics, with claimants in Vienna, Rome, Armenia, and (formerly) Constantinople.

question: Jesus had been arrested in Gethsemane, tried by the high priest Caiaphas, and delivered to the Roman governor Pontius Pilate for the death sentence the Jews could not legally execute themselves. Pilate examined him, found no crime worthy of death, and tried to release him. Custom let the governor free one prisoner at the Passover. Pilate offered the crowd a choice: release Jesus called the Christ, or release a notorious bandit and insurrectionist? Pilate expected they would pick Jesus. The chief priests had stirred up the crowd. What was the name of the bandit they chose to release instead of Jesus?
answer: Barabbas
choices: Barabbas
Bar-Jonah
Bartholomew
Barnabas
context: Matthew 27:15-26. The name Barabbas literally means 'son of the father' in Aramaic — there is ancient textual tradition that his full name was 'Jesus Barabbas' (i.e., Jesus 'son of the father'), making the choice an even sharper one. Pilate then washed his hands in front of the crowd, declaring himself innocent of Jesus's blood. The crowd shouted: 'His blood be on us and on our children!'

question: Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene came alone to the tomb where Jesus's body had been laid the Friday before, bringing spices to anoint the body properly. She found the great stone rolled away. She ran back and got Peter and John, who raced to the tomb. Peter saw the linen wrappings lying there and the head-cloth folded separately. The two disciples went home wondering. Mary stayed by the tomb weeping. She turned around and saw a man she took for the gardener. What was the first word he spoke that made her recognize him?
answer: Mary
choices: Mary
Daughter
Sister
Beloved
context: John 20:1-18. She cried out 'Rabboni!' — Aramaic for 'Teacher.' Jesus told her: 'Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.' He sent her to tell the other disciples. Mary Magdalene was the first witness of the Resurrection — significant because under first-century Jewish law a woman's testimony was not legally admissible, suggesting the Gospels are reporting something embarrassing they would not have invented.

question: On the evening of the Resurrection, ten apostles were gathered behind locked doors in fear of the temple authorities. Jesus suddenly stood among them, said 'Peace be with you,' and showed his hands and side. But Thomas, called the Twin, was not there. When they told him later 'We have seen the Lord!' Thomas insisted he would not believe unless he could put his finger into the nail marks and his hand into the spear-wound. A week later Jesus appeared again, with Thomas there. What did Jesus tell him to do?
answer: Put your finger here and reach your hand into my side
choices: Put your finger here and reach your hand into my side
Be silent until you have heard the others speak first
Wash your hands in the basin and come to the table
Lay your sword down before you approach my body
context: John 20:24-29. Thomas answered: 'My Lord and my God!' Jesus replied: 'Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.' Thomas later, according to tradition, took the Gospel to India and was martyred there; the Mar Thoma Christians of Kerala trace their church to him. The phrase 'doubting Thomas' for a skeptic comes from this story.

question: At the Last Supper Jesus warned Peter: 'Before the cock crows tonight, you will deny me three times.' Peter protested he would die first. That night Jesus was arrested and led to the high priest's house. Peter slipped into the courtyard, sitting by the fire. A servant girl said: 'You were with Jesus.' Peter denied. Another said it. He denied again. A third bystander said his Galilean accent gave him away. Peter cursed and swore he did not know the man. What happened next?
answer: The cock crowed, and Jesus turned and looked at Peter
choices: The cock crowed, and Jesus turned and looked at Peter
The high priest stepped out and recognized Peter aloud
Judas Iscariot returned to throw the silver pieces back
The chief priest's torch went out in a sudden gust
context: Luke 22:54-62. Peter went out and wept bitterly. After the Resurrection, on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, Jesus deliberately asked Peter three times: 'Do you love me?' — three questions for three denials. Each time Peter said yes, Jesus told him: 'Feed my sheep.' Tradition holds that Peter was eventually crucified upside-down in Rome under Nero around 64-67 AD, refusing to be crucified the same way as his Lord.

question: Stephen, one of seven deacons appointed by the apostles to aid Greek-speaking Christian widows, was full of grace and power, working signs among the people. Synagogue members could not stand up to his wisdom in argument. They bribed false witnesses and dragged him before the Sanhedrin on charges of blasphemy. He reviewed Israel's history and accused his judges of murdering the Righteous One their prophets had foretold. The crowd dragged him outside and stoned him. As the stones fell, what did Stephen see?
answer: Jesus standing at the right hand of God
choices: Jesus standing at the right hand of God
Twelve angels carrying a scroll above the heavens
His own mother in heaven robed in white linen
The temple curtain torn in two as at the cross
context: Acts 6-7. Stephen prayed: 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit' and 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them' — echoing Christ's own words from the cross. A young Pharisee named Saul of Tarsus stood watching, holding the cloaks of the killers, approving the killing. That same Saul would later be struck down on the road to Damascus and become the Apostle Paul.

question: Being transported as a Roman prisoner to face Caesar, Paul boarded a grain ship from Alexandria with 276 people aboard. He warned the captain not to sail late in the season; they sailed anyway and were caught by a hurricane-force northeaster off Crete that drove them helpless for fourteen days. They threw cargo, tackle, and finally the wheat overboard. At dawn on day fifteen they ran aground on Malta. While Paul gathered firewood, a viper struck him on the hand. What happened next?
answer: Paul shook the snake off into the fire and was unharmed
choices: Paul shook the snake off into the fire and was unharmed
The viper turned into a smooth white branch in his hand
Paul healed the bite with prayer and oil from a vessel
The viper bit him again and Paul fell into a deep sleep
context: Acts 27-28. On the fourteenth night an angel had told Paul no lives would be lost. The Maltese people, expecting Paul to swell up and drop dead, watched him for hours and then concluded he must be a god. Paul stayed three months on Malta and healed the father of the chief Roman official Publius from fever and dysentery. He then sailed on to Rome on another grain ship, the *Castor and Pollux*, where Christians from Rome came out forty miles down the Appian Way to meet him.

question: The angel Gabriel was sent by God to a town in Galilee called Nazareth, to a young virgin betrothed to a carpenter named Joseph, of the house of David. The angel said: 'Greetings, favored one! The Lord is with you.' Mary was troubled. Gabriel told her she would conceive and bear a son, name him Jesus, and he would reign over Jacob's house forever. Mary asked: 'How can this be, since I am a virgin?' Gabriel gave her one sign about her elderly relative. What was the sign?
answer: Her elderly relative Elizabeth was six months pregnant
choices: Her elderly relative Elizabeth was six months pregnant
Her cousin Anna had received a vision in the temple
Her uncle Zechariah had been made high priest at Jerusalem
Her sister Salome had been chosen as the first witness
context: Luke 1:26-38. Gabriel said the Holy Spirit would come upon her and the power of the Most High would overshadow her. Mary answered: 'Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word' — the *fiat* that defines Mary in Christian devotion. The angel departed. Mary then went immediately to visit Elizabeth in the hill country of Judea; the unborn John leaped in Elizabeth's womb at Mary's greeting, and Mary sang the Magnificat: 'My soul magnifies the Lord, my spirit rejoices in God my Savior...'

question: After Jesus was born in Bethlehem in the days of King Herod, magi from the east came to Jerusalem asking: 'Where is the one born King of the Jews? We saw his star.' Herod, alarmed, asked his priests where the Messiah was to be born. They said Bethlehem. Herod sent the magi on with a private order to report back. They found the child, presented their three gifts, were warned in a dream, and went home another way. What did Herod do when he realized he had been outwitted?
answer: Ordered every boy in Bethlehem two years old and under killed
choices: Ordered every boy in Bethlehem two years old and under killed
Sent soldiers to burn the stables at the village edge
Had his palace astrologers blinded for failing to find the star
Sealed Bethlehem's gates and let no man pass for one year
context: Matthew 2. The episode is the Slaughter of the Innocents. Joseph had been warned in a dream and had taken Mary and the child to Egypt; they returned only after Herod's death. The magi's gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh are the basis for the tradition of three magi, though the Gospels don't say how many. They are not called kings until later tradition. Herod the Great died in 4 BC; the actual birth was probably 6-4 BC, not the conventional zero of the calendar.

question: Travelling toward Jerusalem along the border of Samaria and Galilee, Jesus entered a village where ten men suffering from leprosy stood at a distance (the law forbade them from approaching the healthy). They called out from across the field: 'Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!' Jesus simply told them to go show themselves to the priests, as the law required for a healing to be certified. As they went, all ten were healed. But only one came back, falling at Jesus's feet to thank him. What was special about the one man who returned?
answer: He was a Samaritan, a foreigner
choices: He was a Samaritan, a foreigner
He was a Roman soldier of Capernaum
He had been a leper longer than the others
He was the youngest of the ten by many years
context: Luke 17:11-19. Jesus asked: 'Were not ten cleansed? Where are the other nine? Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?' He told the Samaritan: 'Rise and go, your faith has made you well.' The story turns on the contrast between the religious insider and the despised outsider — a major Lucan theme that also appears in the Good Samaritan parable.

question: A scholar asked Jesus how to inherit eternal life. Jesus turned it back: love God, love neighbor. The lawyer pressed: 'And who is my neighbor?' Jesus told a story. A man traveling from Jerusalem to Jericho fell among robbers who beat him and left him half-dead. A priest passed by on the other side. A Levite did the same. Then a Samaritan, whom Jews despised, was moved with pity, bandaged the man with wine and oil, brought him to an inn, and paid the innkeeper. What did the Samaritan promise the innkeeper?
answer: I will pay whatever more you spend when I come back
choices: I will pay whatever more you spend when I come back
Send word to my house and I will return at once
Take this gold ring as security for further cost
If the man dies, bury him at my expense in your yard
context: Luke 10:25-37. Jesus asked the lawyer which of the three was the neighbor to the man who fell among robbers. The lawyer would not even say the word 'Samaritan' — answering simply: 'The one who showed him mercy.' Jesus said: 'Go and do likewise.' The road from Jerusalem to Jericho was famously dangerous — descending 3,300 feet through desert wadis — and the story is set against the real bandit-infested geography.

question: Jesus told of a man with two sons. The younger asked for his share of the inheritance early, took it, traveled to a far country, and squandered everything on reckless living. When his money ran out, a famine struck. He hired himself out to feed pigs and was so hungry he longed to eat the pigs' bean-pods. He came to his senses: even his father's servants had bread to spare. He resolved to go home, confess, and beg to be made a servant. While he was still a long way off, what did his father do?
answer: Ran out, embraced him, and kissed him
choices: Ran out, embraced him, and kissed him
Waited at the gate until his son finished kneeling
Sent the older brother to bring him inside the house
Turned away weeping at the sight of his ruined son
context: Luke 15:11-32. The father ordered the best robe, a ring for his finger, sandals for his feet, and the fatted calf killed for a feast. The older brother, returning from the field, was furious — he had served faithfully for years and never been given so much as a young goat. The father pleaded: this brother of yours was dead and is alive again, was lost and is found. The parable, central to Luke's Gospel, is sometimes called 'the Gospel within the Gospel.' Pope Francis declared a 'Year of Mercy' built around it.

question: Teaching in the Jerusalem Temple in the last week of his life, Jesus sat across from the treasury watching the crowd drop money into the offering boxes. The wealthy gave large sums conspicuously. Then a poor widow came up and dropped in two small copper coins. Jesus called the disciples together and said: 'Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all the others.' Why, according to Jesus, had she given more than all the rich?
answer: They gave out of abundance, but she gave all she had to live on
choices: They gave out of abundance, but she gave all she had to live on
Her coins were the oldest currency, from the reign of David
She had walked all night from Galilee to make the offering
Her husband's debts had just been remitted by the priests
context: Mark 12:41-44 and Luke 21:1-4. The coin was the *lepton* (Greek for 'small') — also called a 'mite' in the King James, the smallest Roman-era bronze coin in circulation. Two lepta made a *quadrans* — about 1/64 of a denarius (a day's wage). Jesus's comment immediately follows his denunciation of the scribes who 'devour widows' houses' (Mark 12:40) — making her the deliberate object lesson against religious greed.

question: Passing through Jericho on the way up to Jerusalem, Jesus drew his usual crowd. Zacchaeus, chief tax collector of the district and wealthy, wanted to see Jesus but was too short. He climbed a sycamore tree to wait. Jesus reached the tree, looked up, called Zacchaeus by name, and told him to come down because Jesus must stay at his house that day. The crowd grumbled that Jesus was eating with a sinner. What did Zacchaeus then declare to Jesus at his own table?
answer: Half of all I own goes to the poor; I will repay any I cheated fourfold
choices: Half of all I own goes to the poor; I will repay any I cheated fourfold
I will leave my house and follow you from this hour onward
I have given a tenth to the temple every year for ten years
If you stay one night, my whole household will become disciples
context: Luke 19:1-10. The tree was a sycamore-fig — known in Hebrew as *shikma*, with broad lower branches that made it climbable. Jesus said: 'Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham — for the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.' Tax collectors in Roman Palestine were collaborators and often defrauders; the fourfold restitution Zacchaeus offered was the maximum the Mosaic law required only for stolen animals.

question: Captured as a teenage boy by Irish raiders from his Christian Roman-British home around 405 AD, Patrick was kept six years as a slave herding sheep on a remote Irish hillside before escaping back to Britain. Years later he became a missionary bishop and returned willingly to the same Ireland that had enslaved him. Tradition holds he stood before the High King Laeghaire at Tara and used a common roadside plant to explain the Christian doctrine of three Persons in one God. What plant did he pluck and hold up?
answer: A shamrock — three leaves on a single stem
choices: A shamrock — three leaves on a single stem
A holly branch — a single leaf with three sharp points
An oak leaf — three veins from one stem to its tip
A trefoil clover — three white petals on each flower
context: The shamrock legend appears in late-medieval sources rather than Patrick's own *Confession* (his autobiographical Latin letter, written near the end of his life around 460-490 AD). Patrick's *Confession* describes his capture, escape (he walked 200 miles to a ship), and call to return to Ireland through a dream of 'the voice of the Irish' calling him. The shamrock became the national emblem of Ireland; St. Patrick's Day on March 17 is the traditional date of his death.

question: Tradition records that Saint Patrick spent the forty days of Lent in 441 AD fasting on the summit of a 2,500-foot mountain in County Mayo overlooking Clew Bay — the same mountain pilgrims still climb barefoot each year on the last Sunday of July. From there Patrick is said to have driven a great host of demons in the shape of black birds into the sea below. Patrick was tempted, harassed, and finally rewarded by an angel of God with the promise that he himself would judge the Irish on Judgment Day. What is the name of that mountain?
answer: Croagh Patrick
choices: Croagh Patrick
Ben Bulben
Slieve Mish
Mount Brandon
context: *Croagh* is the Irish word for 'mountain' or 'rounded peak.' The mountain was a pagan holy place dedicated to the harvest god Lugh long before Patrick climbed it; Reek Sunday pilgrims still walk barefoot up the steep scree to the summit chapel. The annual climb draws tens of thousands. The local nickname for the mountain is 'The Reek.'

question: In 1429 a peasant girl in Lorraine, who had been hearing the voices of Saints Catherine, Margaret, and the Archangel Michael since age thirteen, convinced the French dauphin Charles to give her armor and an army to break the English siege of Orléans. Joan of Arc was seventeen. She wore white armor and carried her own banner painted with Jesus and Mary. Wounded by an arrow at the great fort of Les Tourelles, she pulled it out, returned to the field, and led the final charge. How long did it take her to break a siege the English had laid for six months?
answer: Nine days
choices: Nine days
Three weeks
Six weeks
Three months
context: Orléans was relieved May 8, 1429. The dauphin was crowned King Charles VII at Reims Cathedral on July 17, 1429, with Joan standing beside him holding her banner — having marched the army 100 miles through hostile territory to make it happen. Joan was captured at Compiègne the next May, sold to the English, tried at Rouen, and burned at the stake May 30, 1431, just nineteen years old. She was canonized in 1920.

question: Captured at Compiègne in May 1430 and sold to the English for ten thousand livres, Joan of Arc was tried for heresy at Rouen by a French court packed with English partisans, led by Bishop Pierre Cauchon. She was charged with wearing men's clothing, hearing unauthorized voices, and refusing to submit to Church judgment. She was burned alive on May 30, 1431, just nineteen. After her body was consumed, the English ordered something done with her ashes specifically to prevent French Catholics from collecting relics. What did they do?
answer: Threw her ashes into the Seine
choices: Threw her ashes into the Seine
Buried them in unmarked ground outside the city
Sealed them in lead and dropped them at sea
Scattered them in three forests of Normandy
context: Joan's last word at the stake was 'Jesus' — repeated several times. Witnesses, including her executioner Geoffroy Therage, later said her heart did not burn — he had to throw the ashes of the heart into the river separately. A retrial in 1456 declared the original verdict null and void. Joan was canonized in 1920 and is one of the four patron saints of France.

question: On December 29, 1170, four knights of King Henry II of England rode into Canterbury Cathedral. They were responding to the king's outburst at his Christmas court about Archbishop Thomas Becket — once Henry's closest friend, then bitterly opposed over Church-versus-Crown authority. The knights demanded Becket come with them. He refused, ready to die for the freedom of the Church. They drew swords on the cathedral steps as monks watched in horror. What had the king said in his rage that the knights took as a royal order?
answer: Will no one rid me of this turbulent priest?
choices: Will no one rid me of this turbulent priest?
He must be silenced before the Christmas feast
Let his blood run in the cathedral to teach all
I want him dead by my own birthday next month
context: The knight Reginald FitzUrse struck the first blow. Becket was canonized just three years later, in 1173. His shrine at Canterbury became one of medieval Europe's greatest pilgrimage destinations — the destination of the pilgrims in Chaucer's *Canterbury Tales*. Henry II did public penance in 1174, walking barefoot to the cathedral and being whipped by the monks at Becket's tomb. The shrine was destroyed by Henry VIII in 1538; the saint's bones were burned and the gold and jewels carried off in twenty-six wagons.

question: The son of a wealthy cloth merchant in Assisi in central Italy, the young Francis Bernardone had been a party-goer until illness pushed him toward extreme piety. He began giving away his father's expensive cloth to the poor; his furious father Pietro dragged him before the bishop's court in Assisi's town square in 1206, demanding he return the goods and renounce his inheritance. In front of the entire town, what did Francis do?
answer: Stripped off all his clothes and handed them back naked
choices: Stripped off all his clothes and handed them back naked
Knelt reciting the Lord's Prayer until his father struck him
Threw his money pouch at his father's feet and walked out
Cut off his hair with a knife and burned it before his father
context: Bishop Guido of Assisi covered the trembling young man with his own cloak. Francis went off to live as a beggar and a rebuilder of ruined chapels — refounding the church of San Damiano outside Assisi with his own hands. He preached to crowds, founded the Franciscan Order in 1209, received the stigmata on Mount La Verna in 1224, and died in 1226 lying naked on bare earth as he had vowed. He is the patron saint of animals and ecology.

question: In the summer of 386 AD, a 31-year-old rhetoric teacher named Augustine sat weeping under a fig tree in his Milan garden, racked by a crisis over his addiction to sex and his inability to commit to the Christian faith of his mother Monica. He heard the voice of a child in a neighboring house singing a phrase he had never heard in any children's game. He took it as a divine command, opened Paul's letters at random, read Romans 13:13-14, and the agony lifted. What was the child singing?
answer: Tolle, lege — Take it and read
choices: Tolle, lege — Take it and read
Domine miserere — Lord, have mercy
Sursum corda — Lift up your hearts
Veni Spiritus — Come, Holy Spirit
context: Augustine's *Confessions* (Book 8, around 397-400 AD) is the source. The phrase from Paul: 'Not in carousing and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality... but put on the Lord Jesus Christ.' Augustine was baptized by Bishop Ambrose at the Easter vigil the next year (387). He went on to become Bishop of Hippo in North Africa and one of the four Latin Fathers of the Western Church; his *Confessions* and *City of God* shaped Christian thought for the next thousand years.

question: Around 285 AD, a wealthy young Egyptian Christian named Anthony heard the Gospel reading in church one Sunday — 'If you would be perfect, sell what you have and give to the poor' — and took it literally. He gave away his inherited estates, placed his sister with a community of virgins, and went into the Egyptian desert to live as a hermit. He spent twenty years walled up alone in an abandoned Roman fort at Pispir. Tradition records demons assailing him there in countless forms. What is Anthony known as today?
answer: The father of Christian monasticism
choices: The father of Christian monasticism
The first martyr of the desert
The patron saint of fortresses
The hermit of the upper Nile
context: Anthony's biography, *Life of Antony*, was written around 360 AD by his disciple Athanasius and circulated widely in the late Roman world — it was the book Augustine's friend Ponticianus described to him in Milan, helping push Augustine toward his own conversion. Anthony's temptations became one of the most-painted scenes in Western art (Hieronymus Bosch, Michelangelo, Salvador Dalí). He died in 356 AD reportedly aged 105.

question: Catherine of Alexandria was, by tradition, an 18-year-old Christian princess of remarkable learning who in the early 300s confronted the pagan Roman emperor Maxentius over his persecution of Christians. Maxentius sent his fifty greatest pagan philosophers to argue with her; she converted them all. He had them burned. He offered marriage if she would renounce Christ; she refused. He ordered her broken on a spiked torture device — but when she was placed on it, the device flew apart and killed the onlookers. He then beheaded her. What is the torture device called today?
answer: The Catherine wheel
choices: The Catherine wheel
The Roman rack
The iron maiden
The wheel of George
context: The fireworks 'Catherine wheel' — a pinwheel that sprays sparks as it turns — is named for the saint's torture device. Catherine is one of the four 'Virgin Martyrs' particularly venerated in the medieval West; she was one of the saints whose voices Joan of Arc heard. Her body was said to have been carried by angels to Mount Sinai, where the monastery of Saint Catherine — founded by the Emperor Justinian around 565 AD — still stands and houses the oldest continuously-operated Christian library in the world.

question: Sebastian, by tradition, was a young Roman officer of the Praetorian Guard around 283 AD, secretly a Christian, who used his position to encourage Christian prisoners to die rather than recant. When his faith was discovered, the emperor Diocletian sentenced him to death. He was bound to a stake and shot with so many arrows that a chronicler called him a 'hedgehog.' Left for dead, he was found alive by a widow named Irene, who nursed him to health. What did Sebastian do once recovered?
answer: Returned to the emperor in person to denounce the persecution
choices: Returned to the emperor in person to denounce the persecution
Fled to Spain and lived out his life as a hermit
Gathered soldiers in secret to plot a Christian revolt
Boarded a ship for the Christian community at Ephesus
context: Diocletian had Sebastian clubbed to death and his body dumped into the Cloaca Maxima — the great sewer of Rome. The story of the arrows surviving the first execution made Sebastian a favorite Renaissance subject (Mantegna, Botticelli, Guido Reni) — his pierced body became almost the iconic 'beautiful suffering' image of European painting. He is one of the patron saints of Rome and was invoked against plague — arrows being a traditional image for divine pestilence.

question: Lawrence was a deacon of the Roman Church in 258 AD, charged with caring for the treasures of the Church. When the emperor Valerian ordered the Roman prefect to seize those treasures, the prefect gave Lawrence three days to gather everything. Lawrence used the three days to distribute everything to the poor of Rome. He then assembled the city's poor and crippled in the courtyard and announced: 'These are the treasures of the Church.' The enraged prefect had him roasted on an iron grill. What did Lawrence say halfway through?
answer: Turn me over, this side is done
choices: Turn me over, this side is done
Let the fire be hotter, I do not feel it
Pray I may die before my brothers see this
I forgive you, as Christ forgave the soldiers
context: Lawrence is the patron saint of cooks (a black joke), comedians, and Rome itself. His feast day is August 10. The Perseid meteor shower, which peaks in mid-August, is called in some traditions 'the Tears of Saint Lawrence' for the way the shooting stars seem to fall around his feast. The grand basilica of San Lorenzo fuori le mura ('Saint Lawrence outside the walls') in Rome stands where tradition says he was buried.

question: Saint George, by tradition, was a Roman officer executed under Diocletian around 303 AD for refusing to renounce his faith. In the legend shaped by the *Golden Legend* (1260), George rode out to Silene in Libya, terrorized by a poisonous dragon. The citizens had been feeding it two sheep a day; when sheep ran out, they drew lots to feed it their children. The lot fell on the king's daughter. As she stood weeping by the pond in wedding finery, George rode up. What did he do with the dragon?
answer: Speared it but kept it alive, leading it on the princess's belt
choices: Speared it but kept it alive, leading it on the princess's belt
Cut off its legs and burned the body on the shore
Drove it into the pond and sealed it with a great stone
Bound it in golden chains and rode it to his ship
context: George then promised to kill the dragon publicly only if the king and all his people would convert to Christianity. They did — fifteen thousand baptisms. The legend made George the patron of soldiers; he is the patron saint of England (adopted by Edward III), Georgia, Catalonia, Portugal, Ethiopia, and Moscow. The cross of Saint George is the red cross on white background on the English flag and the center of the Union Jack.

question: Stephen, full of grace and power, was the first follower of Jesus killed for his faith. False witnesses dragged him before the Sanhedrin on charges of blasphemy against the temple. He defended himself by reviewing Israel's history of resisting its own prophets and accused his judges of murdering the Righteous One the prophets had foretold. The Sanhedrin covered their ears, rushed at him, dragged him outside the walls, and stoned him. As the stones fell, who is named in Acts as holding the cloaks of the killers and approving the killing?
answer: A young Pharisee named Saul of Tarsus
choices: A young Pharisee named Saul of Tarsus
A scribe named Eliezer ben Jared
A Sadducee named Ananias the priest
A Roman tribune named Claudius Lysias
context: Acts 7:58. That same Saul would later be struck down on the road to Damascus, baptized, and become the Apostle Paul — the very Stephen-killing he had supervised may have been part of what drove the conscience-stricken zealot toward conversion. Stephen's last words, 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit' and 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them,' echoed Jesus's own words from the cross. His feast is December 26, the day after Christmas.

question: In 325 AD the Roman emperor Constantine, recently converted and urgently wanting the Church unified, summoned every bishop in the empire to Nicaea (in modern Turkey) to settle a quarrel tearing the Church apart. The Alexandrian priest Arius taught that Jesus, though divine, was a created being subordinate to the Father. His opponent was the young deacon Athanasius, who insisted the Son was fully and eternally God. The council sided with Athanasius and produced a creed Christians still recite. What is the name of the creed it produced?
answer: The Nicene Creed
choices: The Nicene Creed
The Apostles' Creed
The Chalcedon Creed
The Athanasian Creed
context: The fight was not over for decades — Constantine's later sons supported Arian bishops, and Athanasius was exiled five times totaling seventeen years on the run. Athanasius died Bishop of Alexandria in 373 AD, leaving behind the final form of the New Testament canon as we have it (his Easter letter of 367 lists the same 27 books). The Visigoths, Vandals, and Lombards who later invaded the Empire were all Arian Christians — the dispute shaped Europe for centuries.

question: Tradition records that during his missionary work in Ireland in the mid-400s, Saint Patrick climbed Croagh Patrick in County Mayo and fasted there for forty days. On the summit he is said to have driven every serpent in Ireland into the sea below — using a wooden bell or, in some versions, his bishop's crosier. Ireland has been famously free of snakes ever since. What is the actual reason no native snakes live in Ireland?
answer: It was glaciated, then separated by sea before snakes could spread
choices: It was glaciated, then separated by sea before snakes could spread
Medieval monks killed every snake brought in by traders
Its acidic peat soil is hostile to reptile reproduction
Snakes never crossed the Pyrenees northward into Europe
context: Patrick's *Confession* makes no mention of snakes; the legend grew up in the medieval Lives. The literal absence of native Irish snakes is genuine — Ireland was buried under ice during the last glaciation, then separated from Britain by rising sea levels before snakes could spread there as they did across the rest of Europe. The 'snakes' Patrick drove out have long been read as symbolic — the pagan Druidic religion he confronted and converted.

question: According to the *Little Flowers of Saint Francis* (c. 1330), the Umbrian town of Gubbio was terrorized by a huge wolf that had killed sheep, dogs, and several townspeople. Francis, visiting Gubbio, walked alone out the gate. The wolf charged with jaws open. Francis made the sign of the cross and addressed the wolf as 'Brother Wolf,' calling him to peace. The wolf lay down at his feet. Francis then brokered a treaty. What were its terms?
answer: Gubbio would feed the wolf daily; the wolf would harm no one
choices: Gubbio would feed the wolf daily; the wolf would harm no one
The wolf would leave Gubbio forever; the town would build a chapel
The wolf would be baptized and live in the bishop's own stable
The townspeople would pray three times daily for the wolf's soul
context: The wolf lived peacefully among the people of Gubbio for two more years before dying of old age, going from door to door for its food. The townspeople wept at its death. In 1873 the skeleton of a large wolf was actually found buried under the floor of a Gubbio church — giving the legend an unusually concrete archaeological footnote. Francis's affection for animals, including his preaching to birds, founded the long Catholic tradition of blessing animals on his feast day, October 4.

question: In 155 AD, the elderly bishop Polycarp of Smyrna was hunted down at a country house and brought into the city stadium under arrest. The Roman proconsul gave him the standard out: curse Christ and burn incense to the emperor, and live. Polycarp was 86 years old. The proconsul threatened him three times — fire, beasts, the sword. Polycarp answered with one line that became one of the most-quoted in early Christian witness. What did he say?
answer: Eighty and six years I have served Him, He never did me wrong
choices: Eighty and six years I have served Him, He never did me wrong
My faith is older than your empire and will outlast your stones
Let the fire come, I have already buried it in my own heart
I would feed your beasts before I feed the demons in your temples
context: The *Martyrdom of Polycarp* (c. 156 AD) is the earliest detailed account of a Christian martyr's death outside the New Testament. The full quote: 'Eighty and six years I have served Him, and He never did me wrong — how can I now blaspheme my King who saved me?' Witnesses reported that the flames bent away from him in an arch like a sail, so a soldier finally stabbed him with a sword. Polycarp was a disciple of the Apostle John — one of the last direct human links between the New Testament generation and the post-apostolic Church.

question: Around 723 AD, the Anglo-Saxon missionary Boniface was converting pagan Germanic tribes in Hesse and Thuringia. The chief obstacle was their veneration of a massive ancient oak at Geismar, sacred to the thunder god Donar (the Germanic Thor). Boniface gathered a crowd of armed hostile pagans around the tree, took an axe, and began chopping. He had barely struck the first blow when a great wind split the oak top to bottom — it fell in four pieces, no person was hurt, and many pagans converted on the spot. What did Boniface build from the wood?
answer: A chapel dedicated to Saint Peter
choices: A chapel dedicated to Saint Peter
A pulpit for his missionary preaching circuit
A monastery school for Frankish children
A wooden cross fixed in the empty stump
context: The chapel at Geismar became the seat of the bishopric of Fritzlar. Boniface went on to organize the Frankish Church under Pope Zachary, anoint Pepin the Short as king of the Franks (founding the Carolingian dynasty that produced Charlemagne), and was finally martyred by pagan Frisians at Dokkum in 754 AD — they came after his payroll, but found only the books he had brought to read. The book he was reading when killed (cut by an axe through its cover) is still preserved at Fulda.

question: Born into the royal Uí Néill family of Donegal around 521 AD, the Irish monk Columba (Colmcille) was an ordained priest who fell into a violent quarrel with another monk over the copying of a Psalter — the dispute escalating into a battle between two royal clans at Cúl Dreimhne in 561 AD, in which thousands died. Wracked with guilt, Columba imposed exile on himself: he would not return to Ireland until he had won as many souls to Christ as had died in the battle. He sailed north with twelve companions and founded a monastery in 563 AD. On what island?
answer: Iona
choices: Iona
Mona
Bute
Mull
context: Iona became the missionary base from which Celtic Christianity spread across Scotland and northern England — its daughter monastery Lindisfarne in turn re-evangelized Anglo-Saxon Northumbria. Columba died on Iona in 597 AD, the same year Pope Gregory the Great sent Augustine to evangelize the Anglo-Saxons of Canterbury from the south. The island lies off the Isle of Mull's western tip. The illuminated *Book of Kells*, possibly begun at Iona before Viking raids forced its move to Ireland, is one of the supreme treasures of medieval European art.

question: The young Roman nobleman Benedict, born around 480 AD, abandoned his studies in Rome to live as a hermit in a cave at Subiaco. His holiness attracted disciples. Eventually a community of monks at nearby Vicovaro begged him to be their abbot. Benedict's discipline was too strict for them. The monks plotted to poison him at a meal — handing him a cup of poisoned wine. According to his biographer Gregory the Great, what happened when Benedict made the sign of the cross over the cup?
answer: The cup shattered in his hand as if struck by a stone
choices: The cup shattered in his hand as if struck by a stone
The wine inside turned cloudy and gave off a foul smell
A black raven flew through the window and overturned it
His hand grew so heavy he could not lift the cup to his lips
context: Benedict left Vicovaro and founded Monte Cassino around 529 AD, where he wrote his famous *Rule* — the document that organized Western Christian monasticism for the next 1,500 years. Its motto, *ora et labora* ('pray and work'), shaped European culture from the dark ages through the high middle ages. Monte Cassino was destroyed four times — by Lombards (581), Saracens (883), an earthquake (1349), and Allied bombing in World War II (1944). It was rebuilt each time. Benedict's twin sister Scholastica founded the parallel female order; the Order of Saint Benedict still operates worldwide.
